fields.Text: A relational database can only use {{c1::tables}}, {{c2::rows}}, {{c3::columns}} and {{c4::cells}}.
Design goes from the real world (mini-world) to a {{c1::model (ER diagram)}} to a {{c2::relational database}}.
An entity type becomes a {{c1::table}}; its attributes become {{c2::columns}}; each entity becomes a {{c3::row}}; its key becomes the {{c4::primary key}}.

fields.Front: Map PROFESSOR (EmpID, LastName, FirstName, Office, Ext).
fields.Back: PROFESSOR(EmpID, FirstName, LastName, Office, Ext) with primary key EmpID; rows such as Laura Reid 11 ST238 86905.

fields.Front: Library example: write the tables for Book, Publisher and Member.
fields.Back: Book(Book_ID, Title, Price, Author, Available); Publisher(Pub_ID, Name, Address); Member(Member_ID, Member_date, Member_price, Address, Name, Expiry_date).

fields.Front: How is a composite attribute mapped when creating an entity's table?
fields.Back: Include only its simple component attributes (e.g. First and Last, not Name).

fields.Front: What is the stated objective of the mapping-entities video?
fields.Back: Look at an ER diagram and figure out how to turn each entity into a table.

fields.Front: How does the instructor map the composite attribute Name(FirstName, LastName) of PROFESSOR?
fields.Back: Name itself does not become a column; only its pieces FirstName and LastName become columns.

fields.Front: What counting habit does the instructor use before mapping the library ER diagram?
fields.Back: Count entities to get the number of tables (3), then count each entity's attributes to get its columns: Book 5, Publisher 3, Member 6.

fields.Text: In the PROFESSOR table, {{c1::6}} professors give 6 rows and {{c2::5}} attributes give 5 columns; each column describes something about that professor.

fields.Front: What does the instructor call 'the first rule I want you to get from this'?
fields.Back: Once you have your ER diagram, each entity becomes a table and the attributes become the columns.
